findings.title: Else-clause raises after batches are already committed, and misfires when cleanup finished exactly at the cap
findings.evidence:
Loop body commits each batch (`db.commit()`), breaks only when `cursor.rowcount < batch_size`, then the for-else block does:
        raise RuntimeError(
Two problems: (1) reaching the cap means up to MAX_BATCHES * batch_size rows are already deleted and committed, yet the caller gets an exception with no deleted count and no rollback, so a caller cannot distinguish partial success from total failure; (2) if the table holds exactly MAX_BATCHES * batch_size matching rows and that count is an exact multiple of batch_size, the last full batch is committed, the loop exhausts without ever breaking, and a completed, correct cleanup is reported as a failure.
findings.recommendation: Only raise when there is evidence of remaining work: after the loop, run a cheap existence probe (e.g. SELECT 1 ... WHERE where_sql LIMIT 1) or treat a final rowcount == batch_size as an extra iteration check rather than an error. On the cap path, include the number of rows already deleted in the exception (or return a truncated-result dict) and document that committed batches are not rolled back.

findings.title: qmark LIMIT placeholder does not match the stated MySQL dialect
findings.evidence:
The module comment claims `MySQL dialect` and the statement appends the limit as a bound positional parameter,
            tuple(params) + (batch_size,),
while the SQL uses the qmark `?` style. MySQL drivers (mysqlclient/PyMySQL) use the format paramstyle and will not bind `?` in a DELETE ... LIMIT clause; conversely SQLite only accepts DELETE ... LIMIT when compiled with SQLITE_ENABLE_UPDATE_DELETE_LIMIT, and this is exactly the driver whose paramstyle is qmark. So on either backend a plausible driver/statement pairing breaks at runtime rather than at call time.
findings.recommendation: Pick one dialect and make it explicit: either use the driver's paramstyle consistently (e.g. format style for MySQL) and raise on unsupported drivers, or assert the DELETE...LIMIT support at startup. Add a test that executes the batched delete against the real target driver.

findings.title: Mandatory-filter guard only checks for a non-empty string, so a tautology bypasses it
findings.evidence:
if not where_sql or not where_sql.strip():
The stated guarantee is a mandatory filter, but any non-blank fragment passes, including `1=1` (whole-table wipe) or stacked statements such as `1=1; DELETE FROM sessions`. Table names are allow-listed, but the predicate itself gets no structural validation, so the guard protects against forgetting the argument, not against a wrong one.
findings.evidence_quote: if not where_sql or not where_sql.strip():
findings.recommendation: Require callers to pass a structured predicate (column, operator, value) or have them supply a fixed SQL template from an allow-listed set; at minimum reject fragments containing `;`, comments, or a bare constant and require the dry-run path to be exercised before any live run.

findings.title: Per-batch commit also commits unrelated caller work and leaves the in-flight batch unrolled-back on error
findings.evidence:
db.commit()
The function commits the connection it was handed after every batch. If the caller passed a shared connection with other pending changes, those are silently committed as a side effect of cleanup (API contract surprise); and if `db.execute` raises mid-loop, the previously committed batches stay applied while the failing batch is left to the caller's connection state, with no explicit rollback.
findings.recommendation: Require a dedicated connection/transaction for cleanup (or take a commit callback), and wrap each batch in an explicit try/except that rolls back the failing batch before re-raising with the accumulated deleted count.
